newsitem.title: UK: Irish, British ministers discuss peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Irish, British ministers discuss peace talks.

text.p: British and Irish ministers met on Friday to try to maintain the momentum towards all-party talks on the future of Northern Ireland despite a new row over proposals for guerrilla groups to give up weapons.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who on Thursday evening published the text of a letter she had written on the subject to Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, met Irish Foreign Affairs Minister Ray Burke in London.

The two sides were expected to discuss the anger of pro-British unionist parties at Britain's terms for allowing Sinn Fein to take part in the talks on the British province's constitutional future planned for the autumn.

In her letter, written on July 9, Mowlam told Sinn Fein chief negotiator Martin McGuinness his party could join the talks provided there was first "a genuine and unequivocal IRA ceasefire which is seen to be matched by word and deed".
The Irish Republican Army abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February last year, resuming its 28-year struggle for a united Ireland.

Mowlam said once Sinn Fein entered the talks, it could remain in them provided it respected principles of non-violence and democracy already set out by talks chairman George Mitchell, a former U.S. senator.
But the negotiation would proceed alongside discussions about the "decommisioning" of weapons held by the Irish Republican Army and other guerrilla groups.

David Trimble, leader of Northern Ireland's largest Protestant party, the Ulster Unionists, had a stormy meeting on Thursday with British Prime Minister Tony Blair, telling him these ideas would not put enough pressure on the IRA to disarm.

"It is absolutely essential from our point of view that there are clear commitments to actual disarmament that will be endorsed by the British government, the Irish government and all the parties to the negotiations," he told reporters after the 70-minute meeting.

If Protestant parties vote against proposals for decommissioning at a meeting between the two governments and Northern Ireland parties other than Sinn Fein next Wednesday, the whole talks strategy could be in jeopardy.
Mowlam and Burke, who were joined in the London talks by Irish Justice Minister John ODonoghue, were expected to give a news conference at about 1130 GMT.
